claims.text: Factory's Missions system breaks large work into focused units handled by fresh agents with narrowly scoped goals, shared state, and explicit validation, because a single agent's context window cannot hold most real projects.

Factory's design rationale is that agents are highly reactive to their context: a trajectory is append-only, models seek coherence, and irrelevant or adversarial accumulated context degrades performance.

In Missions the orchestrator plans and decomposes the user's goal, delegates all investigation and implementation to subagents and workers, and does not drive validation directly; the system injects validators at milestones.
Missions workers complete well-specified features with clear success criteria and write tests before code, but an independent validator, not the worker, makes the final judgment on correctness.
Missions validators do not implement fixes; they surface issues to the orchestrator, which creates fix features that future workers implement.

At the mission level the orchestrator writes a validation contract (behavioral assertions defining success) before defining any features, so the contract is not influenced by the planned implementation.
Missions state is externalized into shared artifacts: validation-contract.md, features.json, services.yaml, AGENTS.md, research notes, operational guidelines, and an evolving knowledge base.
A programmatic runner spawns one fresh-context worker per feature in order; when all features in a milestone are complete, the runner triggers validation with fresh agents.

Missions uses two validator types: scrutiny validators review each worker's implementation and trajectory and encode knowledge updates into shared state, and user-testing validators exercise the system as a black box against the validation contract.

After validation, the orchestrator creates targeted fix features that run before the milestone re-validates, looping until validation passes; if implementation or validation is blocked, the orchestrator halts the mission and returns control to the user.
Missions allows model choice per role: broad planning and judgment for the orchestrator, reliable and cost-efficient execution for workers, and thoroughness and skepticism for validators.
A Slack-clone mission ran 16.5 hours: orchestration 2.3%, implementation 60.5%, validation 37.2% of runtime, with 185 total agent runs (63 workers, 27 validators).
The Slack-clone mission used 778.5M tokens (744.9M cache read) and produced 38.8k lines of code, 52.5% of them tests, with 89.25% statement coverage.

In the Slack-clone mission every milestone converged in 2-4 validation rounds; validators surfaced 81 issues (65 blocking) and the orchestrator created 21 fix features, 34.4% of 61 implementation features.
In the Slack-clone mission median trajectory length was 51 turns for implementation (p90 123) and 30 turns for validation (p90 37).

Custom droids are Markdown subagents with their own system prompt, model, and tool policy, and each invocation runs in a fresh context window through the Task tool, returning a single final message to the parent.
Subagents run non-interactively: the AskUser tool is disabled and a subagent cannot spawn its own subagents because the Task tool is unavailable to it.
Droid ships built-in droids `worker` (all tools, default medium complexity) and `explorer` (read-only, default light complexity).

The Task tool accepts subagent_type, description, prompt, optional complexity (light/medium/heavy), run_in_background (returns a task_id, fetched via TaskOutput, stoppable via TaskStop), and resume to continue a prior subagent with full context preserved.
Subagent autonomy defaults to inheriting the parent's level, is clamped to the organization's Maximum Autonomy Level, and subagents with tools: read-only never run above Low.

Subagent model resolution order is: model pinned in droid frontmatter, then complexity-to-model routing, then parent's model, with fallback to the parent's model if a pinned model is blocked by org policy.

`droid exec` is a one-shot headless mode that is read-only by default, with edits and commands opt-in via --auto low/medium/high, and it exits non-zero at the first action exceeding the autonomy level.
`droid exec --worktree` runs a task in an isolated git worktree on its own branch to fan out parallel jobs; clean worktrees are auto-removed on exit and dirty ones preserved.

Factory's Deferred Context Engine loads tool schemas, MCP schemas, skills, and plugin instructions only when needed, cutting estimated input tokens 15.1% on average (39.4% p90) in MCP-triggering sessions and 50.8% on average for sessions with 100+ deferred tools.
Factory's Code Droid technical report claimed 19.27% on SWE-bench Full and 31.67% on SWE-bench Lite (300 problems) pass rate on first attempt.
